title: What to check when your weight loss stalls
chunks: A true weight-loss plateau is when your weekly average weight has genuinely not moved for 2–3 weeks or more, despite consistent effort. A few flat days, or a single stalled week, is normal fluctuation — not a plateau — so judge it on multi-week averages before changing anything.

Before cutting calories, rule out hidden intake. Tracking creep is the most common culprit: portions drift larger, oils and sauces go unlogged, weekend meals get estimated. Tighten up by weighing foods in grams and logging everything for a week or two — this alone restarts most stalls.

Remember that maintenance calories fall as you lose weight: a smaller body burns less. The deficit that worked at the start may now be roughly maintenance. This is expected, not 'broken metabolism,' and it means your target needs a small downward adjustment over time.

Check water retention before assuming fat loss has stopped. Stress, poor sleep, high sodium, a new training stimulus, and hormonal cycles can hold water for weeks and mask real fat loss underneath. Sometimes patience, better sleep, and a few low-stress days reveal a 'whoosh' of progress.

When a stall is real, you have two main levers: slightly reduce calories (by about 100–200 kcal) or slightly increase activity (more daily steps or a bit of cardio). Increasing activity lets you keep eating more, which many people find easier to sustain.

Consider whether a diet break is the right move instead of cutting further. After many weeks of dieting, 1–2 weeks at maintenance can reduce fatigue and improve adherence, setting up better progress when you resume — especially if energy, sleep, and mood have suffered.

Avoid the trap of slashing calories ever lower and adding endless cardio. That path is unsustainable and can harm muscle and wellbeing. Make small, measured adjustments, give each 2–3 weeks to show, and keep protein and training high throughout.
